claims.statement: IMDT members agree to actively provide and promote force-free training methods and reject methods or equipment that may cause physical or mental discomfort.
IMDT members agree to avoid positive punishment and negative reinforcement as tools for training dogs.
IMDT members agree to work within professional limits and refer owners to a suitable professional when needs exceed those limits.
In the UK, animal trainers, training instructors and behaviourists are not regulated by government; anyone may use those job titles regardless of training or experience.
ABTC requires registered trainers, instructors and behaviourists to use science-based methods and keep up to date with research-informed thinking.
ABTC states it does not agree with aversives being used to train animals and publishes an indicative list of aversive equipment and methods that should not be used.
Positive reinforcement training means giving the dog something they want when they behave in a way the owner likes, making that behaviour more likely in future.
When starting a new skill, Dogs Trust advises rewarding the dog every time they are successful; reward type and schedule can change after the behaviour is reliable across environments.
A marker signal must always be followed by a reward so the dog can be confident they got the behaviour right.
Undesired behaviour may increase if the dog receives attention, eye contact or interaction as a consequence—even when the owner intends to discourage the behaviour.
Before training new behaviours, the dog should learn that the marker predicts a reward via repeated marker-then-treat pairings.
Dogs Trust advises saying a verbal marker as calmly as possible because excited delivery can excite, confuse or distract the dog.
Dogs Trust advises teaching reliable name response before adding a formal recall cue.
Dogs Trust advises giving the dog at least five seconds to respond to a recall cue before calling again, and not repeating the cue if the dog is unlikely to return.
If a dog ignores recall during training, Dogs Trust advises staying calm because anger or shouting can reduce willingness to return; use long line guidance or collect the dog instead of punishing.
Dogs Trust advises off-lead exercise in open spaces only when the owner is confident the dog will come back when called.
Dogs Trust states that in the UK dogs in public should wear a collar and ID tag and have up-to-date microchip details, as required by law.
RSPCA states all dog training should be reward based, using food, toys or praise when the dog shows desired behaviour.
RSPCA recommends breaking training into short but regular sessions and starting new tricks in a quiet room with minimal distractions.
RSPCA recommends looking for ABTC-registered animal training instructors for ethical training that meets welfare needs.
RSPCA advises owners not to join classes if techniques rely on fear, pain, choke chains, shouting or hitting.
RSPCA advises adding the verbal cue 'sit' only as the dog moves into sit, not before, to avoid associating the word with the wrong movement.

In Hiby et al. (2004), the number of owner-reported problem behaviours correlated with the number of tasks trained using punishment (P<0.001) but not with tasks trained using rewards (P=0.17).
Hiby et al. (2004) conclude that punishment may represent a welfare concern without concurrent benefits in obedience within the pet-owning community surveyed.
